title: Zone Plate
short_intro: A zone plate is an optical device based on the principle of diffraction and constructive interference, designed to focus light without refraction. It consists of a series of concentric annular regions, known as Fresnel zones, which alternately block and transmit light.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definition of Fresnel zones, radius of zones, comparison with convex lens, and focal length formula.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Phase reversal zone plates, multiple foci of a zone plate, intensity distribution at the focal point, and comparative study with a lens.

concept_notes.heading: Construction and Principle of Zone Plate
bullets: A zone plate is constructed by drawing concentric circles on a glass plate whose radii are proportional to the square roots of natural numbers.
The areas of all Fresnel zones are approximately equal, regardless of their order number n.
Alternate zones are rendered opaque (blackened) so that light waves reaching the observation point from consecutive transparent zones differ in phase by pi radians.

concept_notes.heading: Difference Between Zone Plate and Convex Lens
bullets: A convex lens focuses light using refraction based on Snell's law, whereas a zone plate focuses light using diffraction and interference.
A convex lens has a single principal focus, while a zone plate has multiple foci corresponding to different orders of diffraction (m = 1, 3, 5...).
Chromatic aberration in a zone plate is extremely large because focal length is inversely proportional to the wavelength of light.

concept_notes.heading: Phase Reversal Zone Plate
bullets: Instead of blocking alternate zones, a phase reversal zone plate retards the light passing through alternate zones by a phase of pi (or half a wavelength).
This modification ensures that all transmitted waves reach the focal point in phase, doubling the amplitude and quadrupling the intensity compared to a standard zone plate.
It acts as a phase hologram for a point source.

concept_notes.heading: Multiple Foci and Focal Length
bullets: The primary focal length of a zone plate is given by f = r<sub>n</sub><sup>2</sup> / (n * lambda).
Secondary foci occur at shorter focal lengths given by f<sub>m</sub> = f / m, where m is an odd integer (1, 3, 5...).
The intensity at the primary focus is much higher than at the secondary foci.

derivations.title: Radius of the n-th Fresnel Zone
derivations.conditions: Plane wavefront incident normally on an aperture at a distance b from the screen.
steps: Let S be a source at a large distance, producing a spherical wavefront. Consider a point P at a distance b from the pole O of the wavefront.
The distance from the n-th boundary of the zone on the wavefront to the point P is given by SO + r<sub>n</sub><sup>2</sup> / (2*b) approximately.
The condition for the boundary of the n-th half-period zone is that the path difference between waves from the pole O and the n-th boundary to P is equal to n * lambda / 2.
Equating path difference: r<sub>n</sub><sup>2</sup> / (2*b) = n * lambda / 2.

derivations.title: Focal Length of a Zone Plate
derivations.conditions: Monochromatic light of wavelength lambda incident on a zone plate of radius r<sub>n</sub>.
steps: The general expression for the radius of the n-th zone is r<sub>n</sub><sup>2</sup> = n * lambda * f, where f is the focal length corresponding to distance b.
Rearranging the formula to solve for the focal length f.
Substituting the values of radius and wavelength for a specific zone n.

solved_numericals.question: The radius of the first half-period zone of a zone plate is 0.5 mm for light of wavelength 5000 Å. Calculate the focal length of the zone plate.
solution_steps: Identify given values: r_1 = 0.5 mm = 5 x 10^-4 m, lambda = 5000 Å = 5 x 10^-7 m, n = 1.
Use the focal length formula: f = r_1^2 / (1 * lambda).

solved_numericals.question: A zone plate has 10 zones. The radius of the 10th zone is 2 mm. Find the principal focal length for light of wavelength 6000 Å, and determine the position of the first secondary focus.
solution_steps: Identify given values: r_10 = 2 mm = 2 x 10^-3 m, n = 10, lambda = 6000 Å = 6 x 10^-7 m.
Calculate principal focal length: f = r_10^2 / (n * lambda) = (2 x 10^-3)^2 / (10 * 6 x 10^-7).
Calculate first secondary focus: f_3 = f / 3 = (2/3) / 3 = 2/9 m = 0.222 m.
solved_numericals.answer: Principal focal length = 0.667 m, First secondary focus = 0.222 m

solved_numericals.question: Find the radius of the 4th zone of a zone plate designed to have a focal length of 1 meter for a wavelength of 5890 Å.
solution_steps: Identify given values: f = 1 m, n = 4, lambda = 5890 Å = 5.89 x 10^-7 m.
Use the radius formula derived from focal length: r_n = \sqrt{n * lambda * f}.

assumptions_and_limitations: It is assumed that the distance from the source and screen to the zone plate is much larger than the radius of the zones (b >> r_n).
Zone plates have extremely high chromatic aberration, making them impractical for use with white light in imaging applications.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A zone plate forms images by refraction similar to a glass lens.
common_misconceptions.correct: A zone plate forms images entirely through diffraction and constructive interference.
common_misconceptions.why: It contains no refracting surfaces; alternate zones simply block light to phase-align the rest.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A zone plate has only one focal point like a standard lens.
common_misconceptions.correct: A zone plate has multiple focal points corresponding to different odd integers (m = 1, 3, 5...).
common_misconceptions.why: Higher-order diffraction maxima lead to secondary focal planes closer to the plate.

quick_revision: Zone plate focal length is given by f = r_n^2 / (n * lambda) and is inversely proportional to wavelength.
Radius of n-th Zone: r_n = \sqrt{n \lambda b}
Area of n-th Zone: A_n = \pi r_n^2 - \pi r_{n-1}^2 \approx \pi b \lambda
